beats.trigger: ## Evaluations
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The judge stays fixed; that keeps the loop's score meaningful.
beats.got: A checker that does not change, and a writer that improves against it. I do not yet know what a judge is.

beats.trigger: Start with the judge you saved at the close of Module 5.
beats.got: There is reading, and I am expected to bring something from before.

beats.trigger: **Build** a self-improving eval loop: separate agents generate and judge, the Module 5 judge scores each round unchanged
beats.got: Three verbs, all about tooling. Nothing about people.

beats.trigger: Can agents improve if you define the outcome and let them find the path, or does organisational mess still matter too much?
beats.got: The question is about whether organisational mess gets in the way. That is close to my world.

beats.trigger: the system absorbs the catches without you.
beats.got: The system improves without a person in it. I'd want to know who is still responsible.

beats.trigger: Evals write down what good means so the system keeps applying it when you are not in the chair.
beats.got: An eval is a written-down standard of good that keeps being applied when you're absent. That sounds like a role profile or a quality bar.

beats.trigger: measured judgment, made runnable
beats.got: Last time's work was turned into a reusable checker.

beats.trigger: every claim cites evidence or admits the gap.
beats.got: The floor means nothing made up and everything traceable to a source. That matters for anything HR sends out.

beats.trigger: Two mails both avoid overclaiming; one is forgettable, the other makes the reader act.
beats.got: Correct and useful are different things, and you can write down what useful means. I could do that for people communications.

beats.trigger: If the judge moved, the score means nothing.
beats.got: If the standard keeps changing, the results can't be compared. Sensible, but I read it as process detail.

beats.trigger: You decide which details the system must never miss.
beats.got: A person decides what the system must never get wrong, and that is a values question as much as a technical one.

beats.trigger: A yardstick you rewrite is not a yardstick.
beats.got: This is a 45-minute technical exercise. The line is repeated and I have already taken it in.

beats.trigger: Note what the judge catches; the tactic must learn that.
beats.got: I ran it once by hand and saw what the checker flags. Fine, but a bit mechanical.

beats.trigger: Come back to a tactic tightened by a judge you did not move.
beats.got: I started it and left. The side prompts about parallel search and model training did not connect to anything I care about.

beats.trigger: weak claims marked grounded mean the judge has a blind spot.
beats.got: The checker can pass things that are weak. So I can't just trust a green result.

beats.trigger: And you weren't there.
beats.got: It got better across three rounds while I was away, and the notes show what changed each time. That is somewhat impressive and somewhat unsettling.

beats.trigger: You do not inspect every output; you design the loop and own the yardstick.
beats.got: My job moves from checking each output to owning the standard. I want to know who in my team could do that.

beats.trigger: Take-home: put any judge in a loop that improves the thing it scores.
beats.got: A suggestion to reuse it on another judge. I'm not sure what I would put in it yet.

beats.trigger: That does not mean the work is done.
beats.got: A score of zero flags does not mean the work is finished.

beats.trigger: A flat score is information about the judge, not the work.
beats.got: When the number stops moving, the checker has run out of things to see. That is when a person's judgment needs to come back, and it is the same reason an engagement survey can go flat while morale does not.

beats.trigger: A generator that grades itself passes itself.
beats.got: Nobody has tested the checker. Compare a few outputs by hand against it once. Also, don't let the writer grade its own work.

beats.trigger: No release so far has told anyone what good means in your company.
beats.got: Models will get better at not making things up, but deciding what good means in our company stays with us. That is a real question for the leadership team.

beats.trigger: The destination is not "the human disappears."
beats.got: The humans stay but move up a level, from doing the work to designing the loop. This is the first place the module says anything about people.

beats.trigger: What would have to be true before you let the agent hit send?
beats.got: A list of conditions that must hold before I'd let it send an internal mail. That is a framing I can use with my own team.

beats.trigger: An ungrounded mail is a trust problem. A grounded but vague or tone-deaf mail is a usefulness problem.
beats.got: Two different failures: losing trust and wasting attention. I had only worried about the first.

beats.trigger: Variety in, selection out, memory keeps
beats.got: Generate lots, throw most away, keep what survived. The three stances and four detectors are jargon I have to scroll back for.

beats.trigger: Some categories never go without a human.
beats.got: The right answer is a choice of draft only, review first, send to yourself, or automatic, and some things always need a person. That is a design decision, not a yes or no, which is what I need for the headcount question.

beats.trigger: Two judges now sit on disk: one keeps the work grounded, one steers it toward your standard.
beats.got: I wrote a check for what a good internal mail is, in my own terms. That is something I could show my HR business partners.

beats.trigger: Every clean week is evidence the loop works, and each one erodes your ability to tell when the loop stops.
beats.got: The better it works, the less people look, and then nobody can tell when it breaks. That is a skills-atrophy risk, and it is a people topic.

beats.trigger: If the answer is a month, put one in your calendar.
beats.got: Put a recurring slot in the calendar to read one real output. It is simple and I can do it.

beats.trigger: Your role in the loop is to design the conditions under which the system earns more autonomy, one loop at a time.
beats.got: A summary of eight pieces. The figure did not show for me. Giving the system autonomy gradually sounds reasonable.

beats.trigger: rewrite the generator's tactic file in place, sharpening it beyond what the loop reached
beats.got: Another technical step with the agent editing a file. Nothing here for people.

beats.trigger: If it sounds too kind, ask: *"Which rule did you claim to remove but keep under another name? Quote both lines."*
beats.got: Challenge the agent's summary and make it show its evidence. I like that I'm allowed to push back.

beats.trigger: You design the loop and own the yardstick.
beats.got: Four points I can repeat. The one about owning the yardstick is the one I'd bring to leadership.

beats.trigger: Pick one call that should run through the eval loop before anyone relies on it, and write the trigger into your working notes.
beats.got: Homework: write down five agent calls for Monday and pick one to run through the loop.

beats.trigger: Trust the loop you can inspect.
beats.got: Trust only what you can inspect. Good line to end on.

take_homes: There are two kinds of check. One makes sure nothing is made up. The other defines what good looks like for the reader. I can write the second kind myself for people communications.
When the score goes flat, it means the checker has run out of things to see. Then a person has to read the work and decide, and someone has to keep doing that or the skill fades.
Before an agent sends anything on its own, decide the level: draft only, review first, send to myself first, or automatic. Some categories always need a human.

monday.move: Write down what a good internal people-update mail looks like in five or six plain criteria, and name which categories of message would never go out without a human.
monday.who: Me, then one HR business partner to react to it
monday.when: Monday morning, 45 minutes, then a 20-minute chat with the HBP on Tuesday
monday.stop_condition: If the criteria are too vague for the HBP to apply to a real mail, I stop and rewrite them before involving any tool.
monday.blocker: Anything involving employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked either yet. I'd start with non-personal mails only.

misconception.why: I still think headcount is the real question, and the module never answers it. But it showed that roles move up to designing the loop and owning the standard, and that some work always needs a person. That makes the question 'which tasks' and 'who owns the standard' rather than just 'which roles go'. I'm not convinced yet.

one_line: The middle section on who owns the standard and when a human must stay in the loop is worth a leader's time, but you have to sit through a lot of tool detail to get there, and it never touches headcount.
